parts.latex: Which one of the following relations is a \textit{many-to-one} relation?

solutions.latex:
$y=9x+2$ is a non-vertical line: one-to-one.

$x^2+y^2=1$ is a circle: many-to-many.

$y=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ is the upper semicircle: each $x$ gives one $y$, but $x$ and $-x$ give the same $y$, so it is many-to-one.

$x=4y^2$ is a parabola opening sideways: one-to-many.

figures.cap: graph of a relation through O: upper branch rising from O to the right, lower branch curving back from the left and going to the right below the x-axis

solutions.latex:
The graph passes the horizontal line test: each $y$ value comes from only one $x$ value.

It fails the vertical line test: for $x>0$ one $x$ value gives two $y$ values.

$\therefore$ the relation is one-to-many.

parts.latex: Which of the following is a graph of a one-to-many function?

solutions.latex:
A one-to-many relation has some $x$-value with more than one $y$-value, so a vertical line cuts its graph more than once.

Graph A is a parabola opening to the left: a vertical line to the left of the origin cuts it twice, but every horizontal line cuts it only once, so it is one-to-many.

Graph B is cut by every vertical line and every horizontal line at most once, so it is one-to-one.

Graph C is cut by every vertical line once, but a horizontal line can cut it many times, so it is many-to-one.

Graph D (a circle) is cut twice by some vertical lines and by some horizontal lines, so it is many-to-many.

Hence graph A is the one-to-many graph.

solutions.latex:

In option D, $x=1$ repeats and $y=3$ repeats (from $x=2$ and $x=3$), so it is many-to-many.

In options B and C no $x$ value repeats, so neither is one-to-many.

parts.latex:
Which type of relationship best describes the curve drawn below?

\exfigure{1323_q2_1}

solutions.latex:
A relationship is one-to-one, many-to-one, and so on, according to how many $y$ values match each $x$ value and how many $x$ values match each $y$ value.

A vertical line such as $x=0$ cuts the curve twice, so one $x$ value gives two $y$ values.

A horizontal line such as $y=0$ cuts the curve twice, so one $y$ value gives two $x$ values.

So the relationship is many-to-many (it is not a function, and its inverse is not a function).

Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - (k^2 - 4)x + 1$.

For which of the values of $k$ below is $f(x)$ many-to-one?

solutions.latex:
$f$ is many-to-one when it is not monotonic, that is when $f'(x)$ changes sign.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-(k^2-4)$$
If $k^2-4\le 0$, then $f'(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$ (zero at most at a single point), so $f$ is increasing and one-to-one.

If $k^2-4>0$, then $f'(x)=0$ has two roots and changes sign, so $f$ has a turning point and is many-to-one.
$$\begin{aligned} k=\pm 2 &: k^2-4=0 \\ k=1 &: k^2-4=-3 \\ k=-4 &: k^2-4=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
Only $k=-4$ gives $k^2-4>0$, which is option D.

parts.latex:
What type of relationship is represented by the graph shown below?

\exfigure{1338_q4_1}

solutions.latex:
The graph is the right half of the circle $x^2+y^2=16$, with $0\le x\le 4$ and $-4\le y\le 4$.

A vertical line $x=c$ with $0<c<4$ cuts the graph at two points, so one $x$ value gives two $y$ values.

A horizontal line $y=c$ cuts the graph at only one point, so each $y$ value comes from exactly one $x$ value.

So each $x$ is paired with many $y$ values, but each $y$ with only one $x$.

Therefore the relationship is one-to-many.

parts.latex: The best description of $x = y^2 + 1$ is:

solutions.latex:
The graph of $x=y^2+1$ is a parabola opening to the right.

Each $x>1$ gives two values of $y$, so the relation is one to many, which is option C.

can_use: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

solutions.latex:
The logarithm $\ln u$ is defined only when $u>0$.

So $\ln(x-1)$ needs $x-1>0$.
$$x>1$$
The inequality is strict because $\ln 0$ is undefined, so $x=1$ is excluded. This rules out option B. The answer is option D.

parts.latex:
The function $f(x)=x^4+ax^3-4x^2+bx+6$ has $x$-intercepts $(2,0)$ and $(-3,0)$.

Find the values of $a$ and $b$.

criteria: Writes both equations, or equivalent merit
Writes one correct equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+e^x)(1+e^{-x})\\ &=1+e^{-x}+e^x+e^0\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
Right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=(1+e^x)+(1+e^{-x})\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)\times f(-x)=f(x)+f(-x)$$
criteria: Expands the LHS correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=x^3-(m^2-4)x+1$.

For which of the values of $m$ below is $f(x)$ many-to-one?
can_use: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is many-to-one when the cubic has two stationary points, that is, when $f'(x)=0$ has two real roots, so the discriminant of $f'(x)$ is positive.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-(m^2-4)$$
$$\Delta=b^2-4ac=0+12(m^2-4)$$
Now $\Delta>0$ requires:
$$\begin{aligned}12(m^2-4)&>0\\m^2-4&>0\\(m+2)(m-2)&>0\end{aligned}$$
Hence $m>2$ or $m<-2$.

Only $m=-4$ satisfies this, so the answer is option A.
